newsitem.title: CHINA: Ericsson sees 30 mln cellphones in China by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Ericsson sees 30 mln cellphones in China by 2000.

text.p: Swedish telecommunications group Ericsson expects the number of cellular telephones in China to reach 30-35 million by the year 2000, up from around six million at the end of 1996, an official said on Friday.

Nael Salah, Ericsson general manager in charge of China's central and eastern regions, said in an interview that his company saw the China telecommunications market growing at least 10 percent a year for the foreseeable future.
Ericsson's managing director Lars Ramqvist told a news conference in Germany on Thursday that China would be the firm's largest market by the end of 1997, topping U.S. sales.

Salah declined to give profit or turnover figures for Ericsson's business in China, but said China accounted for about 10 percent of the company's worldwide sales of 124.27 billion Swedish crowns ($16 billion).
"It is essential for all telecom suppliers to have a presence in China even though the market is very competitive," he said.
Salah estimated the market for Ericsson products in China at about $13 billion for 1997, including $2 billion for handphones.
"The digital handset market is expanding the fastest, about 100 percent expansion every year," he said.
Ericsson is a major supplier of telephone switching systems, digital network equipment, and cellular handphones.
Salah estimated that at present around 55 percent of cellular phone users in China are connected to Ericsson digital systems and 40 percent to Ericsson analog systems.
He said Ericsson had about 10 percent of the China market for switching systems, 17 percent for PABX exchanges for businesses, and 45 percent of the handset market.
"Our estimate is that the total number of cellular subscribers in China by the end of the decade will be 30-35 million, compared to six million subscribers at the end of 1996," Salah said.
"The Ministry of Post and Telecommunications have previously estimated the number to reach 20 million, but will probably agree with our number," he added.
Salah said he saw China's telecommunications market, currently highly controlled by the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications (MPT) and its subsidiaries, becoming more flexible before too long.
"There will be more deregulation soon, giving consumers more choice. Things are happening very fast in China. The MPT has taken steps to ensure more competition in the market," he said.
Portable phones are now mostly sold by MPT or its nominees, but he said other companies will soon be given permission to start sales.
"Ericsson has recently signed an agreement with the MPT under which Ericsson portable phones will be sold in 360 outlets inside post offices around China within two years," he said.

Ericsson's production in China is growing quickly. It now has the capacity to produce all of its switching systems locally, and will this year produce 800,000 digital handsets in China compared with 260,000 last year.

Chinese producers are becoming key players in the switching business, accounting for about 20 percent of China sales in 1996, but Salah said he did not see Chinese companies challenging the major foreign firms in the digital phone field for some time.
"Not yet in the cellular area, it will take a few years," he said.
The company has built up its infrastructure in China fast in the past few years and now have nine joint ventures with a tenth to be opened in the central city of Wuhan next month, he said.
Ericsson's total staff in China, including JV's, is just under 3,000 of which about 300 are expatriates.
